passages.content: *Amd* means "pillar," and *aʾimad* means "pillars." Just as a house stands firm on pillars (columns), so the faith is expressed in summary through these mysteries, and the faithful, by learning these mysteries, live steadfast.

**Mystery (*mistir*)** means something that is kept for a certain time, known only to certain people; in this lesson of ours, however, it means understanding the invisible mystery of the faith through visible symbols, and receiving invisible grace through a visible service.

**Five:** Their number has been fixed at five only on the basis of the word found in 1 Samuel 17:40 and 1 Corinthians 14:19; the fact that these are five, and the wondrous works done through them, explain their role as symbols of the Five Pillars of Mystery.
We will examine these mysteries in order.
*Sillasie* is derived from the Geʽez verb *sellese*, "he made three"; *Sillasie* means "Threeness" (Trinity). In this lesson we learn the Unity and Trinity of God.

When we study the teaching of the Mystery of the Holy Trinity, we do so apart from the reasoning of the laws of mathematical formulas. For the spiritual examines worldly wisdom (philosophy), but spiritual wisdom and mystery cannot be reached by the investigation of worldly knowledge. The matter of faith is not material but spiritual; it is known and believed spiritually, from within faith.

"He said, 'Let us make man in our image, after our likeness'" (Genesis 1:26). Since nothing before this word indicates the existence of a creature resembling God, the phrase "in our image…" shows that God has His own image that is more than one. We find it written in Isaiah 40:12 that God needed no helper when He created the world. Therefore "in our image…" expresses His Threeness (His being more than one), while "He said" expresses His Oneness.

"Adam has become like one of us" (Genesis 3:22). Had God not possessed Threeness in Person, in Name, and in Deed, He would have said, "He has become like me." But because "has become like one of us" indicates plurality, it shows us that God is not one only.

Genesis 11:7: "He said, 'Come, let us go down and confuse their language.'" From this word we understand that one is saying "come" to the others. Since it is known that God needs no one's help for His divine work, the fact that one says "come" to the others shows that within Him there are more than two.

Genesis 18:1: "God appeared to Abraham under the tree of Mamre. And Abraham lifted up his eyes and saw three men." By stating the number three, this passage explains that God, in His Threeness, appeared to Abraham in the likeness of men. To make the point clear: it does not say that God appeared to him together with three men, or together with two angels. Neither angels nor men are called by this name (Isaiah 42:8). Whereas up to this point Scripture had indicated only plurality, here it speaks specifically of three, and so it clearly explains that God possesses Threeness.
God is three in Name, in Deed (*gibr*), and in Person (*akal*).
Threeness of Name

It is by being called Father (*Ab*), Son (*Wold*), and Holy Spirit (*Menfes Qidus*). "Go and baptize them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19). The word "the love of the Father, the grace of the Son, the fellowship of the Holy Spirit" clearly explains His Threeness (2 Corinthians 13:14).
His name (that of the Son), His Father's name, and the name of the Holy Spirit are written on them (Revelation 14:1). The passages given above explain the Threeness of God's Name.
The Father is called Father by His own name; He is not called Son or Holy Spirit. All three are called by their own names (*Haimanote Abew* [The Faith of the Fathers], chapter 11, part 1:7).
"*Sillasie*" means Threeness; it is the collective name for the Threeness of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. When we say "*Sillasie*," we mean the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.
Threeness of Deed (Gibr)
*Gibr* means "work" or "action"; in this lesson we see the Threeness of God's Deed: that the Father is Father, the Son is Son, and the Holy Spirit is the One who Proceeds (*seratsi*).
*Ab* means Father: the One who begot the Son (Matthew 3:17). He is also *Asratsi*, the One who caused the Holy Spirit to proceed (John 15:26).
*Wold* (Son) means *teweladi*, the Begotten (the One begotten of the Father) (Luke 1:35). The Holy Spirit means *seratsi*, the One who Proceeds (the One who proceeded from the Father) (John 15:26).

In saying that the Father is Father, the Son is Son, and the Holy Spirit is Breath (Life), the Threeness of Deed expresses the Threeness of the Name. This does not mean, however, that because the Father is called Father and Source (*asgeñ*), He precedes or surpasses the Son and the Holy Spirit; nor is the Son less than the Father, nor less than the Holy Spirit; nor is the Holy Spirit less than the Father and the Son. All are glorified equally, in Unity and in Trinity.
Threeness of Person (Akal)
The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit each have their own perfect face (*gets*), perfect form (*melk*), and perfect person (*akal*).
***Gets*** means the face; it includes the parts of our body visible above the neck: eyes, ears, and the like.
***Melk*** refers to the parts of our body when each is counted individually (foot, hand, head, hair, eye, ear…).

***Akal*** is, in general, the whole of our body. The *akal* of creatures is visible, tangible, measurable, and limited; but the *akal* of the Holy Trinity is invisible, not touched by hand, not limited by place, and fills all things (Psalm 138:7).

The Threeness of God in Person: as revealed in Matthew 3:16, the Father was clearly seen in the cloud, the Son in the flesh He had put on, and the Holy Spirit in the likeness of a dove. Furthermore, His appearing to Abraham in the likeness of three men was to explain to him that He is three in Person. Because the Threeness of the Holy Trinity is distinct from human mathematical formulas, it (*Qidist Sillasie*, the Holy Trinity) is called a unique Threeness. For by the law of mathematics there is nothing that is one while being three… They each have their own Threeness of Name, Deed, and Person.

The Threeness of God is in three things only: in Name, in Deed, and in Person. In everything else He is one: for example, in Nature (*bahriy*), in Existence (*hilwina*) (John 14:8), in Will, in Authority, in Creating… Although we find things written of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit in different works and ranks, this is to express the Threeness of their Name, Deed, and Person; all of them are present in the work of any one. The God who created the world and is governing it, who became man and saved the world, is one only (Ephesians 4:5).

*Kunet* or *kewin* means "state" or "being" (mode of being); this is explained through the analogy of the human soul. The soul, while being one, has three properties (*kunetat*): heart (thinking), word (speaking), and breath (life). If one of the three properties is lacking, it cannot receive the name "soul."

The Threeness of God is presented through the analogy of the human soul: the Father as the heart (thinking), the Son as the word (speaking), and the Holy Spirit as the breath (life). The Father, being heart for Himself, is the heart of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. The Son, being word for Himself, is the word of the Father and of the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit, being life for Himself, is the life of the Father and of the Son. In His Godhead there are heart, word, and life. Just as the soul, though it has three properties, is called one, so God, though He has three Names, three Deeds, and three Persons, is called one God and not three gods (Deuteronomy 6:4; Malachi 2:10).
The Sun

The sun has a body (mass), light, and heat. The Father is represented by its body, the Son by its light, and the Holy Spirit by its heat. Just as the sun is one while having three conditions, so God is three while being one, and one God while being three.
Water

Water has volume (extent), wetness, and coolness. The Father is likened to its volume (extent), the Son to its wetness, and the Holy Spirit to its coolness. Just as water is one, so God is three while being one, and one God while being three. There are other creatures as well that are presented as analogies. They serve, however, to teach by way of analogy; the nature of a creature cannot explain the nature of God.
*Sigawie* is derived from the Geʽez word *tesegewe*, "He became man"; *Mistire Sigawie* means the Mystery of becoming man.

**1. To cleanse Adam from his transgression.** When Adam, listening to Satan's counsel, ate of the fig tree (*ʿetse beles*) of which God had told him not to eat, broke His commandment, and became estranged from his Creator, the sentence of death (death of the body and death of the soul) was pronounced upon him (Genesis 3:1). The serpent and Eve, who had been the cause of his fall, were also cursed according to the measure of their offense (Genesis 3:14).

Because Adam acknowledged his fault and repented, God promised him that He would become man and save him (Genesis 3:22). The covenant is the word "Adam has become like one of us," which expresses that God promised that God the Son, in His distinct Name, His distinct Deed, and His distinct Person, would become man and save him.

According to the promise He had made to Adam, when the time came He became man in order to free him (to save him) from the sentence pronounced upon him (Galatians 4:4). "The time" means five thousand five hundred (when five and a half days were fulfilled) (Psalm 89:4).

**2. To make amends for the transgression of the flesh.** Adam transgressed the divine word, "In the day that you eat of the fig tree you shall surely die" (Genesis 2:17), by eating of the fig, and the sentence of death was pronounced upon him. After this, because he repented, God willed to forgive him without annulling His judgment, "you shall die." Therefore, since death does not befit His divine nature, it was in order to put on mortal flesh (to become man) and receive the punishment on Adam's behalf (Isaiah 53:1). And because goodness is of God's very nature, it was His will, by dying Adam's death and fulfilling the judgment, and by forgiving and showing His goodness, to reveal both His judgment and His forgiveness at once.

**3. To reveal His love.** However much we humans love a person, we can give material things; and even that, we do with an eye to our own benefit (profit). But our God, though He would gain nothing from us, humbled His nature, united Himself with our weak nature, took upon Himself the sentence pronounced on Adam, and saved us, because He willed to reveal His true love to us (John 15:13; John 10:11; Isaiah 40:11).
**1.** Before the time of His birth arrived, dwelling in the prophets, He had symbols foreshadowed and prophecy spoken.
Symbols
The priesthood of Melchizedek: Melchizedek is a symbol of the Lord; Abraham, of the faithful (Genesis 14:18; Hebrews 7:1).
The lamb sacrificed as a ransom for Isaac (Genesis 22:18): Isaac is a symbol of Adam; the lamb, of the Lord (John 1:29).

The manna of Israel (Exodus 16:13): Israel is a symbol of Adam; the manna, of the Lord (John 6:32). Egypt is a symbol of Sheol (*Siʾol*); Canaan, of the Kingdom of Heaven; the Red Sea (*Bahire Ertra*), of sin; the rod of Moses, of the Cross; and there are many other symbols as well.
"May God dwell in the house of Shem" (Genesis 9:26): the one called "God" is the Son; the "house" is Our Lady.
"In your seed all the nations shall be blessed" (Genesis 22:18): the one called "seed" is the Lord; those called "nations" are humankind (Galatians 3:16).
"A star shall come forth out of Jacob" (Numbers 24:17): the star is a symbol of the Lord; Jacob, of humankind (Matthew 2:7).

**2. At the hour she received the angel's Annunciation.** When the angel Saint Gabriel brought the good news to Our Lady and she accepted it, saying, "Let it be to me according to your word," He made her word the occasion: uniting His divine nature with the weak human nature, and becoming one *akal* (person) out of two *akal*, and one *bahriy* (nature) out of two *bahriy*, He became perfect man and perfect God. This means that, making His divine nature one with human nature (uniting them), He became man and God (perfect man, perfect God) (Luke 1:30; Matthew 1:23; John 1:14).
**3. And when the union took place:**
***Inbele wulatie*** — without change: not like Lot's wife (Genesis 19:26), nor like the water of Cana (John 2:1).
***Inbele tusahie*** — without confusion: without being mixed as honey and water are; preserving one another, both the Word and the flesh, without their natures being changed.
***Inbele buʿadie*** — without separation: without separation such as that of raw grain; after the Incarnation He abides in union (*Tewahedo*).
***Inbele hidret*** — without indwelling: not like a garment and a box, but in a union like that of fire and iron.

***Inbele tidmirt*** — without addition: not as one object is stacked on another and separated when desired; rather, His Divinity became one with His humanity (*tisibʾit*: the soul and flesh He united to Himself) in perfect union, and so He was born.

God was born of Our Lady, the Holiest of the Holy, the Purest of the Pure, the Virgin Mary; and that He would be born of her was foreshadowed in symbols and foretold in prophecy beforehand through saints guided by the Spirit of God.
Symbols

"May God dwell in the tent of Shem" (Genesis 9:26): the tent is a symbol of Our Lady; "God," of the Lord who became man. The tent of Abraham (Genesis 18:1): the tent is a symbol of Our Lady; the guest who was received in Abraham's house is a symbol of the Lord Himself. The ladder of Jacob (Genesis 28:12): the ladder is a symbol of Our Lady; the King seated upon the ladder, of Christ. The bush of Moses, the green bush and the flame (Exodus 3:2): the green bush is a symbol of Our Lady; the flame, of the Divinity (*Widase Maryam*). The tablets of Moses (Exodus 31:18): the Ark (*tabot*), the dwelling place of the tablets, is a symbol of Our Lady; the tablets, of the Lord. Gideon's fleece and dew (Judges 6:36): the fleece is a symbol of Our Lady; the dew, of the Lord.

passages.content: Prophecy

"She shall be called Eve (*Hewan*)" (Genesis 2:22). *Hewan* means *Imme Hiyawan*, "mother of the living." This name was given in reference to Our Lady. Whereas the first Eve brought death, we call Our Lady *Meserete Hiywet*, the source of life, because the Lord, the Master of life, came forth from her. Psalm 45:4: "The Most High has sanctified His dwelling place." The one called "the Most High" is God; she who is called "His dwelling place" is Our Lady, the Mother of God, who carried Him in her womb for nine months and five days and gave birth to Him.
"A garden locked" (Song of Songs 4:12). This explains that Our Lady gave birth to God in virginity, and her everlasting virginity; furthermore, what is written in Ezekiel 44:1 makes this clear.

"Behold, a virgin shall bear a Son, and they shall call His name Emmanuel" (Isaiah 7:14). This word directly expresses Our Lady's being the Mother of God. For she is the one called "virgin," and the one called "Son" (*wold*, child) is her Son, Emmanuel, Jesus Christ.

In fulfillment of the prophecy of the prophets, He caused Our Lady to be born, through an angel's announcement, of Joachim and Anna, who lived in lawful and holy marriage. She was born in a pure body such as Adam and Eve had before they transgressed, one to which the curse (*tinte abiso*, the first transgression) had not been passed on. Because sin does not befit the nature of the God who would be born of her, and because He who would take upon Himself the transgression of all people had to be pure, and since there is none but God who fulfills this, He made her pure from the curse so that He might be born of her.

Our Lady was conceived on Nehase 7 (Nehase is the twelfth month of the Ethiopian calendar) and was born on Ginbot 1 (the ninth month) in a place called Lebanon (*Libanos*). Because Joachim and Anna had her through a vow, she grew up in the Temple from her third year for about 12 years. When she was 15 years old, the angel Saint Gabriel, sent from God, came and announced to her, "You will give birth to God," and she accepted, saying, "Let it be to me according to your word." Making her word the occasion, God took a portion of her flesh and her soul, united it with His Divinity, and was conceived on Megabit 29 (the seventh month) and born on Tahsas 29 (the fourth month). Thereby He became one *akal* out of two *akal* and one *bahriy* out of two *bahriy*; and it is for this reason that our faith is named Orthodox *Tewahedo* (Union).

As foretold in Micah 5:2, our Lord was born in the town of Bethlehem, in a cattle stall. Because a decree had been issued that all the people should be registered (counted), Joseph took Our Lady and went from Nazareth to Bethlehem to be registered; because of the multitude of people they found no house and lodged in a cattle stall. While they were there, the days of her delivery came, and she gave birth in virginity to Christ, the Savior of the world (Matthew 1:18; Luke 2:1). When He was born, the Magi (*Sebʾa Segel*), concerning whom prophecy had been spoken beforehand, came as far as Bethlehem with a star guiding them, fell down and worshipped Him, and gave Him their gifts (gold, frankincense, and myrrh) (Matthew 2:11).

The shepherds who were in the area also saw the light shining around them, and, with the angel guiding them, reached the cave where the Lord was born and saw the Lord's birth. Together with the angels they sang, *"Sibhat le-Igziʾabher be-semayat we-selam be-midr"* ("Glory to God in the heavens and peace on earth"): praise was given in the heavens, and there was peace on earth, good will to humankind (Luke 2:14).
*Timqet* means being baptized; being dipped; being immersed; going down into and coming up out of water.
Among the things that took place in the Old Testament era and were symbols of the true (*amanawi*) baptism of the New Testament, we shall look at the following.

**The Flood:** The *maye ayh* (waters of the Flood), which in the days of Noah destroyed the people who did not regret their transgression and repent, and all who lived on the earth (except Noah and his family and the creatures kept so that their kind would remain), is a symbol of baptism; and Noah and his sons, who were saved from the Flood, are a symbol of the faithful who are born of God through baptism in the fresh water that flowed from the side of Christ for our baptism, and are saved from judgment (Genesis 7:1; Genesis 19:1; 1 Peter 3:20).

**Circumcision** (Genesis 17:14): For its time, circumcision was a distinguishing mark for Israel according to the flesh (*Israʾel ze-Siga*); its fulfillment, however, is as a symbol of baptism, which was yet to come and which is the glory of the faithful, Israel according to the soul (*Israʾel ze-Nefs*) (Colossians 2:11).

**The Sea of Eritrea (the Red Sea)** (Exodus 14:21; 1 Corinthians 10:1): Moses is a symbol of Christ; the rod with which he divided the sea, of the Cross; the Red Sea, of judgment and of Sheol; and the Israelites who crossed through the divided sea are a symbol of the faithful who, born of God through baptism by His blood shed on the Cross, cross over the sea of sin.

**The waters of the Jordan** (Joshua 3:14; Joshua 4:15): Joshua is a symbol of Christ; the Jordan, of baptism; and the Israelites who crossed the Jordan, of the faithful who are saved by believing in Christ and being baptized.

**The baptism of John** (Matthew 3:1): After John had for some time been baptizing the people with the baptism of repentance, when the Lord came he led them to the Lord, saying, "Behold the Lamb of God." Therefore the baptism of John is a symbol that prepares for the true baptism of the Lord.
It was our Lord who instituted baptism, and the reasons He was baptized are:
To reveal His Oneness and Threeness (the Mystery of the Holy Trinity), which had not been revealed in the Old Testament (Matthew 16:17).
To be an example to us, teaching us how, by whom, and where we ought to be baptized (John 13:12).
To blot out the bond of our debt, which the enemy, the devil, had cast into the Jordan (Colossians 2:14).

Having been baptized at the hand of John, He instituted for us the true baptism, through which we recover the sonship that was taken from us when Adam and Eve ate of the fig tree and transgressed the commandment of their God, and through which we are born of God. After this He showed it to the apostles on the evening of Holy Thursday (*Tselote Hamus*) by washing their feet. For at that hour, when Saint Peter protested, saying, "I should wash you; you shall not wash my feet," the Lord's saying, "If I do not wash you, you have no union with me," makes us understand that baptism is the only way by which we become one with God and are born of the Spirit.
After our Lord instituted baptism for us, we recall what He taught Nicodemus: that we too, being born of water and the Spirit, receive sonship and inherit His Kingdom (John 3:1).

For the apostles, the Mystery of Baptism was accomplished on Holy Thursday; but the Holy Spirit descended upon them on the fiftieth day after the Lord rose, the tenth day after He ascended. After them, when the faithful were baptized, the Holy Spirit was clearly seen descending upon them in the likeness of fire (Acts 2:1; Acts 8:14).
Our Lord was baptized in the Jordan to fulfill the prophecy that had been spoken and the symbol that had been foreshadowed.
Symbols
Abraham's crossing of the Jordan when he returned after defeating the kings of the nations is a symbol of the baptism of the faithful; Melchizedek, of the Lord (Genesis 14:17; Hebrews 6:1).

Israel's crossing of the Jordan and entering their inheritance, Canaan, is a symbol of the faithful, having believed and been baptized, entering their heavenly inheritance, the Kingdom of Heaven (Joshua 3:14).
Elijah's crossing of the Jordan and ascending is a symbol of the faithful, having been baptized, attaining the ascension of the soul (*ʿirgete nefs*) (2 Kings 2:8).
Naaman's being baptized in the Jordan and healed of leprosy is a symbol of the faithful being baptized and healed of the leprosy of the soul (2 Kings 5:14).
Prophecy
"The sea saw and fled; the Jordan turned back; the mountains skipped like bulls" (Psalm 113:3).
Because water is found everywhere: so that people may easily obtain sonship and inherit the Kingdom of Heaven.
Just as water makes withered plants flourish: so that the faithful, being baptized, may obtain the flourishing of the soul.
Just as water cleanses from dirt: so that the faithful, being baptized, may be cleansed from sin (Acts 2:38; Ezekiel 36:25).
Just as water puts out fire: so that the faithful, being baptized, may be saved from the fire of Gehenna (Matthew 3:6–12).
When we are baptized, we obtain remission of the sin passed on to us through the curse (Ezekiel 36:25; Acts 2:38).
When we are born through baptism from the womb of the Holy Spirit (*abrake Menfes Qidus*), our sonship that was taken from us is restored to us (John 3:1).
We are saved from the judgment of the fire of Gehenna spoken of in the word, "He who does not believe and is not baptized will be condemned" (Mark 16:16).
Our being immersed in the water is a symbol of our dying with Christ, and our coming out of the water, of our rising (Romans 6:3).
Through baptism we become one with our Lord (Galatians 3:27) and with the faithful (Colossians 2:11).

All who believed through the preaching of the apostles, of whatever age, were baptized (Acts 16:15; 1 Corinthians 1:16). Later, however, with their parents vowing to teach them, the baptism of children began: males on their fortieth day and females on their eightieth day.

The basis for this is as follows. When children of Israel were born, their parents, on the fortieth day for a male and the eightieth day for a female, would go to the Temple bringing an offering (*mebaʿ*, a gift) for them, register them in the record of Israel (of citizenship), and make them entitled heirs of Canaan, the Land of Promise. In the same way today, with their parents taking responsibility to teach them their faith and a godfather or godmother also making a vow, children are christened (baptized) and inherit their parents' inheritance, the Kingdom of Heaven.

Those who come for baptism after the fortieth and eightieth day, however, may be baptized at any age, after they have learned their faith and believed. As long as they are alive, nothing at any time prevents them from being baptized.

Before being baptized, the candidate must learn the faith properly, believe, and confess it. If the candidate is a child, the parents or the godfather or godmother must come forward and vow to teach him.

When being baptized, he must go down into and come up out of the water three times, for it is a symbol of the death and resurrection of Christ. The candidate is baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19). If the candidates are married and also have a family, all must learn, believe, and be baptized together.

After being baptized, one must receive Communion (receive the Holy Body and Precious Blood). If this does not happen, the baptism does not become living. For the word says, "Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you have no life in yourselves." Each person must receive the Holy Body broken and the Precious Blood shed for his sake, and be cleansed from his transgression. For the sonship we received in baptism is confirmed only when we receive His Body and Blood.
Just as we are born of our parents in the flesh only once, so too we are born of God from water and the Spirit (baptized) only once. Therefore baptism is one; it is not repeated.
Just as circumcision, which was a symbol of baptism, took place only once, so baptism is once (Colossians 2:11).

Because it is a mystery through which we partake of the Lord's Body and Blood, and because the Lord died and rose only once, we are baptized only once (Romans 6:3). If someone baptized in our Church enters another religion and is baptized again, or marries a follower of another faith, then, after he returns in repentance, the *Mets'hafe Qedir* (the Book of Qedir, the rite of purification for one returning to the Church) is prayed over him and he is baptized. This, however, is not called a second baptism but a baptism of repentance.
If anyone who was baptized in any church other than the Orthodox Tewahedo churches (Oriental Churches) comes having believed, he is baptized again.
*Qurban* means any gift (*amha*), sacrifice, or spiritual thing offered to God; in this lesson of ours, however, we learn about the sacrifice of the New Testament (the Body and Blood of Christ).
**The sacrifice of Melchizedek** (Genesis 14:18; Hebrews 5:6; Hebrews 6:1): the bread is a symbol of His Body; the wine, of His Blood; Melchizedek, of Christ; Abraham, of the faithful.
**The Passover of Israel** (Exodus 12:1): death is a symbol of the devil; Israel, of the faithful; the lamb, of Christ.
**The manna of Israel** (Exodus 16:13): the manna is a symbol of the Holy Body and Precious Blood of our Lord; Israel, of the faithful; the cloud, of Our Lady.
**Adam:** Through the sacrifice that our father Adam offered, He promised him that after five thousand five hundred years He would become man and save him (Genesis 3:22; Galatians 4:4).
**Noah:** Through the sacrifice Noah offered, He promised Noah and his sons, by the sign of the rainbow, that He would not again destroy the earth by a calamity (Genesis 9:1; Genesis 9:8).

**Abraham** (Genesis 18:3): Through the sacrifice that our father Abraham offered, he heard the word of promise, "In your seed all the nations shall be blessed"; the one called "seed" was, for that time, Isaac, but its fulfillment was for the Lord.

**Melchizedek** (Genesis 14:17; Psalm 109:4; Hebrews 5:6): Through the sacrifice he offered before God, it was said of him that his priesthood is forever, and he became a symbol of Christ (Hebrews 7:1).

**David** (Psalm 131:11): At the hour he offered sacrifice, it was said to him, "Your son who comes from your loins shall reign on your throne"; this was spoken, for that time, of Solomon, but its fulfillment was for Christ (Psalm 71:1). Others, too, received blessing as they offered their pure sacrifices before God.

In the Old Testament era, the sacrificial offering was made from sheep, cattle, and various animals. In the New Testament, however, animals are not offered as sacrifice (*qurban*) in the sanctuary; all sacrifice has been summed up in the Body and Blood of Christ. It was our Lord Himself who instituted this New Testament sacrifice. On the evening of Holy Thursday, with the twelve apostles present, after first performing the sacrifice of the Law (*Orit*) and bringing it to completion, He blessed the bread and the wine and gave them to them, saying, "This is my Body, which will be broken tomorrow on the Cross, and my Blood, which will be shed; eat and drink" (Matthew 26:26).

Today, when the priest places the bread on the paten (*tsahil*) and the wine in the chalice (*tsiwa*) and blesses them while praying the prayer of the Liturgy (*Tselote Qidasie*), just as at that time, the bread is changed and becomes the divine Body (*Siga Melekot*), and the wine is changed and becomes the divine Blood (*Deme Melekot*). When we receive this Holy Body and Precious Blood, it must be while remembering the suffering and torment He endured for our sake, having made ourselves pure from sin through repentance, and believing that it blots out whatever of our transgression remains after repentance, cleanses us from transgression, and gives us eternal life.

The word in 1 Corinthians 11:23, "Do this in remembrance of me," means that when we receive His Body and Blood we should live remembering the suffering He endured on the square of Calvary for the sake of humankind, and His divine love portrayed in our hearts; for the word "remembrance" indicates something that is not forgotten (Galatians 3:1).

Before our Lord revealed (instituted) this mystery, He taught extensively about the Mystery of the Holy Eucharist in John 6:25–58, saying, "Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you have no life in yourselves. He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life. My flesh is true food, and my blood is true drink (which gives life)."
Even if we depart from this world through death, we obtain in the heavenly Kingdom the eternal life that does not pass away (John 6:54).
We obtain remission of our sins (complete salvation) (Matthew 26:26).
We confirm our union with our Lord and with the saints (1 Corinthians 10:17).
The reason He made His Body of wheat and His Blood of wine is to fulfill the prophecy and the symbol.

**Prophecy:** "I have added gladness to my heart; it abounded more than the fruit of wheat and the fruit of the vine" (Psalm 4:7). This word indicates that the Holy Eucharist, the true, perfect, and eternal medicine, is made with wheat and wine.
**Symbol:** Because Melchizedek, the symbol of Christ, offered sacrifice with wheat and wine, it was to fulfill the symbol (Genesis 14:17).
To explain that, just as food unites with the body, so when we receive His Body and Blood He truly unites with us.
Just as food becomes strength for our body, so His Body and Blood give our soul spiritual strength.
Just as Adam and Eve lost their sonship to God through food, so He might restore our sonship to us through His Holy Body and Precious Blood (Genesis 3:1; John 6:49).
We ought always to receive Holy Communion after we have repented of our transgression; for the remission of our sins is confirmed through Holy Communion (Matthew 26:27).

As long as the faithful are alive, whether man or woman, young or old, they must not be separated from Holy Communion; for this mystery is not restricted by sex or age but is given to all (John 6:54). We must not presumptuously receive His Body and Blood without having regretted and repented of the wrongs we have committed; those who do so are guilty (1 Corinthians 11:27). As for the Holy Communion we receive: our Lord, having hung crucified on the square of Calvary, at the ninth hour by His own authority separated His holy soul from His holy body (John 10:18; John 19:30). He went in His soul to Sheol and returned the souls who were there to Paradise; then He rose, having by His will united His soul with the body that had been three days and three nights in the belly of the tomb. During this time, however (the time when His Body and Blood were separated), the Divinity was not separated from the soul or from the body (1 Peter). Therefore the Body and Blood we receive is that from which the soul was separated and with which the Divinity is united (1 Peter 3:18).
Prophecy
"I lay down and slept; I awoke, for God (my Godhead) sustained me" (Psalm 3:5).
"Let God arise; let His enemies be scattered; let those who hate Him flee before His face" (Psalm 67:1).
"God arose as one who wakes from sleep" (Psalm 77:65).
Symbols
Our Lord said that Jonah's spending three days and three nights in the belly of the whale was a symbol of our Lord's death and resurrection (Jonah 1:17; Matthew 12:40).
His going down into the waters of the Jordan and being baptized was a symbol of His death; His coming up out of the water, of His resurrection.

After our Lord, on Friday at the ninth hour of the day, had by His will separated His holy soul from His holy body, Joseph and Nicodemus, having obtained permission from Pilate, buried Him at the eleventh hour of the day in the tomb that Joseph had prepared for himself.

While His body remained three days and three nights in the belly of the tomb, He went in His soul to Sheol, and after returning the souls held captive there (Adam with his children) to their former place, He united His holy soul and His holy body by His will and rose on Saturday night, toward the dawn of Sunday, at the sixth hour of the night. The Divinity, however (without being divided), was not separated from the soul in Sheol, nor from the body (in the tomb). The time our Lord remained in Sheol in His soul (from the ninth hour of Friday to the sixth hour of Saturday night) is about 33 hours. We understand that, just as He spent 33 years on earth in His body, He remained 33 hours in Sheol until His soul was united with His body and He rose.

That our Lord remained three days and nights in the tomb means this: the time after the eleventh hour on Friday is counted as twenty-four hours and called one day and night; Friday night and Saturday daytime are the second day and night; and the six hours of Saturday night, counted together with Sunday daytime, are the third day and night.

This follows the reckoning in the teaching of *Bahire Hasab* (the Ethiopian computus) that says: *"Meʿalt yishibo le-lelit, we-lelit yishibo le-meʿalt"*: the day draws the night, and the night draws the day (the latter draws the former, and the former the latter).

The resurrection of our Lord is the herald (the firstfruits, *bekur*) of the resurrection of humankind (1 Corinthians 15:20). If we too die a death like His (remaining steadfast in believing in Him), He will raise us in a glorious resurrection like His (Romans 6:5). After our Lord rose on Saturday night, toward the dawn of Sunday, at the sixth hour of the night, He appeared to the apostles on three days. These are:
On the day He rose, Sunday, at the eleventh hour of the day, He appeared to His disciples while they were sitting in a closed house (Luke 24:36; John 20:19).
A week after He rose, likewise while they were in a closed house, He appeared to them again, saying, "Peace be with you" (John 20:26).
On the 25th day after He rose (*Rikbe Kahnat*, "the Meeting of the Priests"), for the third time, He appeared beside the Sea of Tiberias and ate a meal with them (John 21:1–14).

During these times He taught them the Seven Covenants (*Sebatu Kidanat*); then, telling them, "Stay in Jerusalem until I send you the Holy Spirit," on the fortieth day He ascended into heaven from the square of Bethany while they watched; and on the fiftieth day He sent them the Holy Spirit.

All human beings depart from this world through death. Yet when the day of the Coming (the end of the world) that God has determined arrives, all people will rise from their state of death, living. When they rise, some (the righteous) rise to glory, and some (the sinners) to judgment (to be judged for the evil works they did) (John 5:29). Concerning the resurrection of humankind, prophecy was spoken and symbols were foreshadowed beforehand.
Prophecy
"Your dead shall live; the corpses shall rise; for the earth shall bring forth the living" (Isaiah 26:19).
"Many of those who sleep throughout the earth shall awake; some shall go to everlasting life, and some to everlasting shame and misery" (Daniel 12:1–3).
"For He has broken us, and He will mend us; after two days He will save us; and on the third day He will raise us up" (Hosea 6:2).
Symbols
The death of Abel is a symbol of our death (Genesis 4:8); the ascension of Enoch, of our resurrection (Genesis 5:24).

Israel's going down into Egypt is a symbol of our death (Genesis 46:1); their coming out of Egypt and entering Canaan, of our resurrection; for Egypt is a symbol of the grave, and Canaan of the resurrection (the Kingdom of Heaven) (Exodus 14:21).
The death of Lazarus is a symbol of our death, and his rising on the fourth day, of our resurrection (John 11:1–44). There are many other symbols as well that point to the resurrection of the dead.

Man was created not to die but to live. However, through his desire that never says "enough," finding the authority given to him insufficient, he was deceived by the counsel of Satan, who dwelt in the serpent, and was found seeking a divinity that had not been given to him; and so death was decreed upon him. Through the transgression of one man, Adam, death came into the world (Romans 5:12). The sentence of death pronounced on Adam and his children (the whole human race) is twofold: death of the soul (descending into Gehenna) and death of the body (descending into the grave). Death of the soul has been removed for the faithful who, having believed and been baptized, receive this Holy Body and Precious Blood, because it was blotted out by the Blood that Christ our God shed and the Body He broke when He was crucified on the square of Calvary to save humankind. The reign of bodily death, however, continues until all people have come to their end; for authority has been given to it to rule over all (1 Corinthians 15:26).
How the Dead Will Rise
Before the dead rise, the angel will sound the proclamation of the trumpet (*nifhate qern*) three times (1 Thessalonians 4:16).
At the first sound of the trumpet (*nifhate qern*), all the bodily parts of the dead will be gathered together.
At the second proclamation of the trumpet: their bodily parts will be joined together with blood and flesh and become motionless corpses.

At the third proclamation of the trumpet: all human beings will rise carrying the works they did in their lifetime, whether good or evil, men at about thirty years of age and women at about fifteen. When they rise, the righteous will rise resembling their Creator, Christ, and the sinners resembling their chief, the devil.

After this, our Lord will come in *kibebe tisibʾit* (seen in the flesh He put on) and in *girma mengist* (the fearsome majesty of the Divinity), escorted by angels, with the Cross on which He was crucified set before Him. Since the Cross is the sign of judgment, at that time the Jews who unjustly crucified and killed Him on the square of Calvary will be put to shame (Matthew 25:31).

Our Lord likens the righteous to sheep and the sinners to goats. This does not mean that their bodily nature will be changed and they will become sheep and goats; rather, because the works they did while living in this world during their lifetime are presented through the analogy of sheep and goats, it is to explain this.

**Sheep:** they spend the day settled in the place where their shepherd has put them to graze; and the righteous live steadfast in the law that Christ, their true shepherd, has made for them (John 10:1; John 21:15).
**Goats:** they are troublesome to the shepherd and cannot settle in one place; and sinners do not live by the law permitted to them; they are fickle and roaming.
**Sheep:** if they find a little grass, they eat it in harmony; and the righteous, saying, "My livelihood is enough for me," share what they have with the poor and eat.

**Goats:** even while there is grass and leaves for them to eat, they spend the day fighting and grumbling among themselves; and sinners, though they have everything, live quarreling, suing one another, killing one another, coveting what belongs to others, and stealing. **Of the sheep:** their nakedness is covered by their tail; and the sins of the righteous are hidden through repentance.

**Of the goats:** their nakedness is exposed, their tail raised up; and sinners, their disgrace exposed to all, are shameless and brazen, boasting and priding themselves in their disgrace and their evil works. **Sheep:** when they walk, it is with their heads bowed down; and the righteous live with their heads bowed, humbling themselves in humility.

**Goats:** when they walk, it is with their heads held up, looking upward; and sinners live thinking beyond their capacity, swollen with pride, saying, "Let anyone who knows more than we do be put to shame," and belittling the work of others.

**Sheep:** if a wolf or a fox eats one of their companions, they leave the area, fleeing and vanishing. And the righteous, if one among them is snatched away by death, say, "Tomorrow it is our turn," and prepare themselves for repentance.

**Goats:** if a wild beast snatches one of their companions, they turn aside for a while, but afterward, having forgotten it, they are found back in the same area eating the grass and leaves. And sinners, when one among them is snatched away by death, seem to grieve for a while; but after a little time, having forgotten the man who died, they are seen quarreling and suing one another over the wealth and property he left behind.
When our Lord sits for judgment, He will set the righteous on His right and the sinners on His left (Matthew 25:31). Its symbolism is as follows:
The right is quick; for the righteous are quick and diligent in good works.
The left is sluggish; and sinners are sluggish toward good things; it does not suit them.
The right is stronger than the left; and the righteous are strong in good works.
The left is weaker than the right; and sinners, when told, "Fast, pray," cannot do it and grow slack.
The right is suited for work and is upright; for the righteous are upright toward good things.
The left is crooked and not well suited for work; and sinners are crooked in their thinking, do not keep their word, and are changeable in their character.

No one knows when the day will be on which our Lord comes for judgment (Matthew 24:36). The saying that even the Son does not know it, however, refers to God's mode of Threeness (*kewin*, *kunet*): since the Father is Heart, the passing away of the world is thought and known in the Father's being Heart; since the Son is Word, it means that He has not "known" it in His being Word by saying, "Let it pass": He has not spoken it and caused it to pass, nor accomplished it in deed. After the resurrection of the dead, the sky (firmament); the three heavens, *Iyor*, *Rama*, and *Erer*; Sheol; Paradise; the four elements, earth, water, fire, and wind; domestic animals, wild beasts, and birds will pass away. Light and darkness will not pass away: of the 24 hours, the night/darkness will be gathered into the fire of Gehenna, and the day/light into the Kingdom of Heaven. The four heavens, *Tsirha Aryam*, *Menbere Mengist*, *Semay Wudud*, and the Kingdom of Heaven (the heavenly Jerusalem), and the fire of Gehenna, however, will not pass away; they will remain forever (Matthew 24:35).

Finally, saying to the righteous, "Come to me, you blessed of my Father," He will make them inherit the Kingdom of Heaven together with the holy angels (Matthew 22:30). And to the sinners He will say, "Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for Satan and his messengers." After this, their eternal dwelling will be in the fire of Gehenna, the place of judgment and torment, with the devil, their father in deeds, and the demons (Revelation 12:7).

The righteous who dwell in the Kingdom of Heaven, though they have differing glory according to the works they did during their earthly life, are not greater than one another in authority; no one commands another (1 Corinthians 15:41).
